walkthroughs.body_html:
Finance and Accounts — a core area of Business Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Finance and Accounts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Finance and Accounts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Luca Pacioli's 'Summa de Arithmetica' detailing double-entry bookkeeping dates from:

options: Payback
Average rate of return
Net present value
Accounting rate

mcqs.q: Should a project be accepted just because its payback period is short?
options: Gearing measures the number of machines a firm owns.
Not necessarily — payback ignores cash flows after the cutoff and the time value of money; NPV and average rate of return give a fuller picture of worth.
Payback period measures how long customers take to pay invoices.
The investment with the fastest payback is always the best.

mcqs.q: Does a high gearing ratio mean a company is failing?
options: Working capital is the annual wages budget.
Gearing measures the number of machines a firm owns.
No — high gearing means heavy reliance on borrowed funds, which raises risk but can boost returns to shareholders when profits exceed interest costs.
Debt on the balance sheet is always a sign of trouble.

mcqs.q: Is working capital the same as cash?
options: Working capital is the annual wages budget.
Working capital is the money in the till and the bank.
No — working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, including stock and receivables; a firm can have positive working capital yet little cash.
Payback period measures how long customers take to pay invoices.
